levels.title: Bootstrapping with pico-boot
levels.description: Plugin auto-discovery over pico-ioc: what it adds, how to publish your own module, and how to switch it off.

levels.title: What pico_boot.init() adds
levels.description:
A drop-in replacement

pico_boot.init() takes exactly the same arguments as pico_ioc.init() and returns the same container. Before delegating it does three things: it normalises the module list, it imports every package that registers a pico_boot.modules entry point, and it collects any PICO_SCANNERS those modules expose.

It also registers pico_ioc.event_bus for you, because that bus is what carries configuration changes across the ecosystem - modules like pico-resilience fail fast without it.

files.name: app.py
main.py
files.content:
from pico_ioc import init, EventBus
import app

# TODO: boot this app the way a pico app really boots. One import changes, and
# the assertion below starts holding without you registering anything extra.
container = init(modules=[app])

print(container.get(app.Greeter).greet("pico"))
assert container.get(EventBus) is not None, "the event bus should be wired"
print("booted with", len(container.keys()), "keys")

solution.main.py:
from pico_boot import init
from pico_ioc import EventBus
import app

container = init(modules=[app])

print(container.get(app.Greeter).greet("pico"))
assert container.get(EventBus) is not None, "the event bus should be wired"
print("booted with", len(container.keys()), "keys")

hints: pico-boot exports an init() that takes exactly the same arguments as the pico-ioc one.
The event bus is core infra for pico-boot: it registers pico_ioc.event_bus on every boot, so hot config reload works.
from pico_boot import init, and leave the call as init(modules=[app]).

levels.title: Publishing your own module as a plugin
levels.description:
The entry point is the contract

Auto-discovery is not a scan of your filesystem: pico-boot asks Python's package metadata for everything registered under the pico_boot.modules group. In a real project you declare it once in pyproject.toml:

[project.entry-points."pico_boot.modules"]\nmy_plugin = "my_plugin"

and the build back-end writes it into the installed distribution. Here you write that file by hand, so you can see exactly what a wheel leaves on disk - and why a module that is merely importable is not discovered.

files.name: my_plugin.py
main.py
files.content:
import importlib
import pathlib

from pico_boot import init
import my_plugin

# An installed package is not magic: it is a directory of metadata next to the
# code. This is what `pip install` leaves behind, written by hand.
dist = pathlib.Path("my_plugin-0.1.0.dist-info")
dist.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
(dist / "METADATA").write_text("Metadata-Version: 2.1\nName: my-plugin\nVersion: 0.1.0\n")

# TODO: declare the entry point that makes pico-boot pick this module up.
# The group is "pico_boot.modules"; the file format is:
#     [group]
#     name = value
(dist / "entry_points.txt").write_text("")

importlib.invalidate_caches()

container = init(modules=[])

assert my_plugin.Stamp in container.keys(), "my_plugin was not discovered"
print(container.get(my_plugin.Stamp).text())
print("discovered without listing it")

solution.main.py:
import importlib
import pathlib

from pico_boot import init
import my_plugin

# An installed package is not magic: it is a directory of metadata next to the
# code. This is what `pip install` leaves behind, written by hand.
dist = pathlib.Path("my_plugin-0.1.0.dist-info")
dist.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
(dist / "METADATA").write_text("Metadata-Version: 2.1\nName: my-plugin\nVersion: 0.1.0\n")

(dist / "entry_points.txt").write_text(
    "[pico_boot.modules]\nmy_plugin = my_plugin\n"
)

importlib.invalidate_caches()

container = init(modules=[])

assert my_plugin.Stamp in container.keys(), "my_plugin was not discovered"
print(container.get(my_plugin.Stamp).text())
print("discovered without listing it")

hints: The section header goes in square brackets, on its own line.
The left side is the entry point name, the right side the module to import.
[pico_boot.modules] on one line, then my_plugin = my_plugin.

levels.title: Turning discovery off
levels.description:
Why you would ever want less magic

Auto-discovery boots every pico package installed in the environment. That is right for an application and wrong for a test suite: the same test would pass or fail depending on what else happens to be installed next to it.

PICO_BOOT_AUTO_PLUGINS is the switch. Setting it to false keeps the rest of pico-boot's behaviour and skips the entry point sweep. This is exactly what the pico-testing plugin sets for every test, with a marker to opt back in per test.

files.name: my_plugin.py
main.py
files.content:
import importlib
import os
import pathlib

import my_plugin

dist = pathlib.Path("my_plugin-0.1.0.dist-info")
dist.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
(dist / "METADATA").write_text("Metadata-Version: 2.1\nName: my-plugin\nVersion: 0.1.0\n")
(dist / "entry_points.txt").write_text("[pico_boot.modules]\nmy_plugin = my_plugin\n")
importlib.invalidate_caches()

# TODO: a test suite must not depend on which pico packages happen to be
# installed next to it. Make this boot ignore them, without touching the
# metadata above.

from pico_boot import init

container = init(modules=[])

assert my_plugin.Stamp not in container.keys(), "discovery should be off here"
print("keys:", sorted(k.__name__ for k in container.keys() if isinstance(k, type)))
print("auto-discovery is off; only what you list gets in")

solution.main.py:
import importlib
import os
import pathlib

import my_plugin

dist = pathlib.Path("my_plugin-0.1.0.dist-info")
dist.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
(dist / "METADATA").write_text("Metadata-Version: 2.1\nName: my-plugin\nVersion: 0.1.0\n")
(dist / "entry_points.txt").write_text("[pico_boot.modules]\nmy_plugin = my_plugin\n")
importlib.invalidate_caches()

os.environ["PICO_BOOT_AUTO_PLUGINS"] = "false"

from pico_boot import init

container = init(modules=[])

assert my_plugin.Stamp not in container.keys(), "discovery should be off here"
print("keys:", sorted(k.__name__ for k in container.keys() if isinstance(k, type)))
print("auto-discovery is off; only what you list gets in")

hints: It is an environment variable, read when init() runs.
The values that disable it are 0, false, no and off.

levels.title: pico-ioc or pico-boot?
levels.description:
Pick by how many integrations you have

  • pico-ioc directly - one application, no pico integrations, or you want to control exactly what is scanned. Tests are the clearest case: list the modules and nothing else can leak in.
  • pico-boot - as soon as you combine integrations (fastapi, sqlalchemy, celery, resilience). Listing them by hand is a maintenance tax and the event bus is easy to forget.

What it does before delegating

  1. Normalises modules: strings are imported, duplicates dropped.
  2. Adds pico_ioc.event_bus, always - it is core infra, not a plugin, so PICO_BOOT_AUTO_PLUGINS does not disable it.
  3. Imports every pico_boot.modules entry point, unless discovery is off.
  4. Collects PICO_SCANNERS from the loaded modules into custom_scanners.

Every parameter of pico_ioc.init() works unchanged: config, profiles, overrides, observers, custom_scanners.
